Whole cocoons are boiled with the pupa inside to keep the thread continuous. About 5,500 silkworms are needed to produce 1 kg of raw silk. Domestication has also limited them: the domestic silk moth cannot fly and depends entirely on humans to survive, and the species does not exist in the wild.

text.bold: 2. Plucking feathers from live birds causes pain.

paragraph.text: The EFSA panel concluded in 2010 that collecting feathers during moulting, by brushing, can be done without pain, but that plucking feathers causes pain and bleeding, and that under commercial conditions some plucking is unavoidable because not all feathers and not all birds moult at the same time. The practice is banned in the European Union, but it is still documented: in 2022, the organization Four Paws released footage of geese being plucked alive on farms in Poland and reported that almost half of the 35 farms visited were doing it. According to the organization, on breeding farms, where birds live longer, a goose can be plucked many times before slaughter. These figures come from an animal protection organization, and the extent of the problem varies by country and supplier.

text.bold: 3. Confinement limits them and makes them ill.

paragraph.text: Ducks and geese are waterfowl, but in intensive farming they generally live in sheds, often with water only from nipple drinkers. A University of Oxford study of Pekin ducks showed that when they have water they can dip their heads in and wet their feathers with, such as baths, troughs or showers, ducks have eyes, nostrils and feathers in better condition than with drinkers alone. In other words, depriving the birds of bathing water, a common practice for reasons of cost and hygiene, harms their health.
Even when it comes from birds killed for meat, down makes the breeding more profitable (I8).
Synthetic and plant fillings, such as corn fiber and kapok, and fabrics such as viscose, lyocell and recycled fibers serve the same purposes.

Brian Tomasik estimated that, in rich countries, the silk consumed by an average person kills a few hundred silkworms a year. To release the thread from the cocoon, the pupae are boiled, baked, dried, pierced with a needle, steamed or fumigated. It isn't known whether the pupa inside the cocoon feels pain, but the doubt calls for caution, and there are fabrics that don't require killing anyone.

The principle being tested is: "if the material is natural, obtaining it does no harm".
Contradicted by EFSA and by a Council of Europe recommendation
It's true that silk and down are natural, biodegradable materials, and that there are production methods that reduce suffering, such as peace silk and collection during moulting.
But those methods are the minority, and even they depend on breeding animals for production. There are materials that keep people warm and well dressed without that.
